title: We're shooting ourselves in the foot': Fareed Zakaria on Trump's tariffs

text: President Trump's sweeping tariffs on Mexico and Canada are raising enormous concerns over how America is treating two of its biggest trading partners. And it comes as the White House further aligns itself with U.S. adversaries like Russia and its authoritarian leader, Vladimir Putin, all while shifting away from Ukraine and clashing with President Zelensky. Joining us now with CNN's Farid Zakaria, Farid, thank you so much for being here with us. I want to begin with these tariffs. What impact will they have on Americans? Oh, they're very significant. They're very substantial. So if you take American cars, the way over the last 25 years that the car industry has made American cars is to create an integrated supply chain with Canada and Mexico. What that means is some parts are made in Canada, some parts are made in Mexico. A lot is made in the U.S. The parts move back and forth. Because of the tariffs, every time an order part moves, it gets tariff. That's why there are estimates by Anderson and consulting firm that the price will go up maybe eight to nine thousand dollars for an SUV. So what you have is the North American kind of industry is now going to be discriminated against and who's going to benefit the German kind of industry, the Korean kind of industry, the Japanese kind of industry. Because those cars were coming to America tariff free. It's a very strange self-defeating set of tariffs because the U.S. has built over the last 30 years, a really remarkable integrated economy with Canada and Mexico. It's in many ways more dynamic than the European Union. And now we're shooting ourselves in the foot. President Trump for read has repeatedly accused other countries, including U.S. allies of taking advantage of the United States. Why does he think this is the case? Trump is a protectionist to his bone. It was his first political statement. text: Tonight, Kamala Harris urging voters in the key swing state of Arizona to end the Trump era. My opponent is also making his closing argument to America. And you've probably seen a bit of it. It is an argument that is full of hate and division. It is time then to turn the page on Donald Trump. We are done with that. Meet him, brand new polling from CNN shows Harrison Trump neck in neck into other battleground states. Georgia and North Carolina. Harry Anton is out front now at the magic wall. So Harry, pivotal as we know these states, but just put them in context for us in terms of what they could mean. Yeah, I got Georgia. Georgia on my mind is Ray Charles used to say, look, as Jeff was talking about in the last segment, the big blue wall runs through the Great Lake Battleground states. That's Kamala Harris' best path, Wisconsin, Michigan, Pennsylvania. That would get Kamala Harris to 270 electoral votes. But let's just say there's some leakage in that great big blue wall. Let's just say that Kamala Harris loses in Michigan. Well, then she drops below 270 electoral votes. But you know what, get a right back over it. Let's just say we give her the state of North Carolina. She gets up to 271 electoral votes. So the bottom line is the Southeast states can very much sort of prove as a backup path potentially for Kamala Harris. Let's just say we're going to put Michigan back in a blue, but we give Pennsylvania away to Donald Trump. Now Kamala Harris is again south of 270 electoral votes. Well, what can sub in? Well, why don't we give her the state of Georgia? Right? It went blue last time. That gets Kamala Harris well above 270 electoral votes. The bottom line is this. Look, Kamala Harris' best path to 270 electoral votes still runs through that great big blue wall up here in the Great Lakes States. But the Southeast provides this backup tour. One little less nugget. I'll sort of point out to you. You know, we're talking about the importance of Georgia in North Carolina. What was the last time a Republican won without Georgia? You got to go all the way back to 1980. Of course, Jimmy Carter was the Democrat nominee, not a big surprise. He carried us home state. How about North Carolina? You have to go all the way back to 1956. The idea that Donald Trump can win without carrying the state of North Carolina history would suggest that they're not going to happen. All right. So when we look at that too, look, there's been a lot made about a different voting blocks in this country. I know you specifically looked at black voters when it comes to Kamala Harris in both of those states. Why do you say they're warning signs? Why are they're warning signs? Well, I'll tell you why they're warning signs. Let's take a look here. This is Democrat versus Donald Trump among African American voters in Georgia and North Carolina average. You go back to November of 2020. Look at that. Joe Biden carried him by 80 points. Right now Kamala Harris on average in our CNN polls has a lead of just 65 points. If Donald Trump ends up winning in Georgia and North Carolina, it could be because Kamala Harris struggled with black voters in the Southeast just as we've seen throughout the national polling as well, Erica. All right. So look at all this though. Donald Trump campaigning in New Mexico. We talked about this a little bit at the top of the show. Has it got read since 2004 for George W. Bush? Does it make sense for Donald Trump to be there at this stage in the race? I don't really think so. Well, first off, why don't we just point out a few obvious things, right? Let's talk about New Mexico and the results that we've had there recently. Look, the 2020 result. Joe Biden won by 11 points. The 2024 forecast has Kamala Harris winning by seven points. So it's not a particularly close race and more than that. Erica, get this. Even if we flip New Mexico over to red, look, we went from 283 to Kamala Harris getting 278. There are very few electoral votes in New Mexico. I know Donald Trump does some interesting things, but this is certainly one of the other ones as far as I'm concerned. All right, Harry. Thanks. Thank you. Out front now, Democratic Senator Cory Booker, he is supporting Kamala Harris for president Senator Nighttahavi with us this evening. So looking at some of this new scene and polling out today for Georgia and North Carolina, Donald Trump has an edge among likely voters when it comes to bringing the kind of change the country needs. 46% versus 41% for the vice president. And you and I both know statistically they go from a set of modeling where if they who they think is going to turn out. There's nothing usual about this election as I crisscross the country. I am seeing what is the makings of a very different kind of turnout model where there's going to be a lot more participation and a lot of different groups than we normally expect. I think that's almost been conceded by the other side. Most Americans are going to vote for her. But strategically, there's about seven states that she's really working on the ground to get the vote out. And I visited pretty much all of them and have seen just things that I really haven't seen since President Obama ran in his first time. I get people coming up to me that break down in tears just with their sense of joy or their sense of fear about what's at stake. And so I think people understand what's at stake and that's actually moving turnout. And I tell you what, these last few days, I've heard from a lot of leaders in the Latino community who weren't as engaged who are now downright ticked off. And has said, you know, as Papa says, I've had all I can stand on. I can't stand no more. Well, speaking of Latino voters, what we saw this week, there's been so much made, of course, about support among not just Latino voters, but also among black voters. This week, actually, just today for President Obama weighing in. So he spoke on Revannell Sharpton's radio show just a short time ago. I want to play a little bit of what he had to say. You know, the Vice President said earlier this week on the breakfast club, she doesn't see any problem when it comes to support among black men. It really doesn't talk about what the denominator is. How big is that 65 percent when the turnout goes up? You're talking a lot, a lot more people voting. And these last days, something has really shifted. I think that he really touched a longstanding ache and hurt that our communities have for being talked down to demeaned and degraded. It was almost like a reminder. Remember who this guy was? Remember the kind of things he's said going back to the Central Park five, going back to birth arisen, which he led against, against Barack Obama. Do you really trust this guy to have your back when he has done so many things repeatedly all the way up until this Madison Getsquare Garden consistently that has kicked you in the gut, looked down upon you and done things that seem so overtly racist. So I just, I really trust that the most loyal voting base the Democratic party has ever had is in the black community. But right now, I think he's really given people cause to pause and to feel more of a sense of urgency to defend our communities from people who look down on us with such bigoted ways. You released a video with Senator John Tester, who may be the most vulnerable Democrat at this point seeking reelection. I'm going to play a little bit of that. This guy will fight you. I'm going to go out on a limb here and say maybe stuntman is not the best day job. But in all seriousness, when you look at that state, right, and when we look at the state of affairs, when it comes to the Senate and holding out into control, how concerned are you about that uphill climb right now for Democrats? I will always bet on Tester. The reality is his state is about the size, population-wise of the county I grew up here in New Jersey, one of our 21 counties, and people know John Tester. Look, my chief of staff is in Montana right now on the ground. They're closing the numbers on their official polling that you see out there. But more than that, they're bumping into so many Republicans. They just know him, trust him, and believe in him. And what Republicans, I think, have made a mistake. They've been from Wisconsin, the person they have running in, it's Tammy Baldwin to Montana. What they have is they bring these multi-multimillionaires, who are better known in other states, that kind of plop in and try to run these outsiders. John Tester is a real sult of the earth. And the great thing about his reputation in the Senate is, indeed, he will. When it comes to defending Montana, he doesn't care if he's fighting a Democratic Republican, he fights for Montana. So if anybody can win in that state because of their authentically independent spirit, it's John Tester. I am going to ask you one quick question. You said he's catching up in the polling, I believe he said in the state. Does that mean that polling's okay? No, it's not. I mean, he would tell, he has told me, he doesn't give a damn. And he too has run it against the opponent that has said the most vile things about Native Americans and others. And people are responding to that. They want somebody that loves all of Montana, not just certain parts. Senator Cory Booker, good to have you with us tonight. Thank you. Thank you.

text: A day after Iran launched its largest ever ballistic missile attack on Israel. Despite some strikes on Israeli bases, the damage was thankfully minimal. Still, Israel is vowing retribution as President Biden implores the Israelis to not retaliate against Iran's nuclear sites. All of this, as Israel continues, it's campaigned to the North and Lebanon, trying to dismantle the Iran-backed organization, Hizbullah, which the United States considers to be a terrorist group. I'm Jim Shudah, who's in Tel Aviv, and Ben Weedemann in Beirut, Lebanon. And Ben, let's start with you. Your team has turned several loud explosions in Beirut. What exactly is going on in Lebanon right now? Well, what we heard is just a few minutes ago, some sharp blasts. And I'm going to step out of the way. I think you could still perhaps see some of the smoke that's still there. This is the heart of Beirut. This is not the southern suburbs. This is the general area where you will find the prime ministry, and you will find the fortunately currently empty CNN Bureau. As I said, this is the second time since Sunday night that there have been Israeli air strikes outside of the heart of Beirut. And just about 40 minutes before that, we heard three very large explosions from the southern suburbs. And we were just smoking, just wafting all over the city. We did the first strike that was about 40 minutes ago. The Israelis put out a statement that they have struck a target in Beirut details to follow the statement indicated. But this comes after a day in which we've seen intense fighting between hisbullah and Israeli forces on Lebanese soil. And we've heard that at least eight Israeli soldiers have been killed in those clashes. And so we haven't seen sort of the kind of full-scale ground presence by Israeli forces in South Lebanon. Perhaps they're probing at this point, but clearly despite Israel's severe pounding of the southern suburbs of Beirut, rather than a southern part of Lebanon along the border, clearly hisbullah has a sizable presence and is able to challenge Israeli forces. Just one last detail. The Ministry of Health has come out with its death toll over the last 24 hours. 46 dead, 85 wounded, as this war continues. Jake. All right, Ben. What are your sources telling you about how Israel might retaliate? Well, there was a sense, Jake, last night that that retaliation might come within hours of the Israeli, of the Iranian missile barrage on Israel, including here in Tel Aviv. That past, of course, last night passed and we're getting quite late here as well. It appears that Israeli leaders may have taken a pause on this decision as they decide the next course. They made it quite public that they attend a response, serious consequences. But there is also some communication going back and forth between Tel Aviv and Washington about how that retaliation takes shape with both private and very public messaging right up to President Biden indicating the U.S. does not want Israel to go so far as to attack Iran's nuclear facilities that the U.S. fears that strike. And by the way, this is not a new fear of the U.S. that that strike would greatly expand this war and might, frankly, drag the U.S. into an open conflict between Israel and Iran that the U.S. does not want to be a part of. And it's quite interesting, Jake, because just as U.S. officials were telling me when Israel sent those ground forces into southern Lebanon or when Israel took out Hassan Nasrallah, just as they were telling me then, they were not involved in those strikes. They're signaling quite clearly now that the U.S. would not be involved in an Israeli strike on Iranian nuclear facilities if it were to choose that path. All right, Jim Sidob and Weedemann, thank you so much to both of you. Stay safe. Joining us now to discuss retired U.S. Air Force General Philip Breedlove, the former NATO Supreme Allied Commander of Europe General. Thanks so much for joining us. So Israel is warning that it has the means to strike anywhere in the Middle East. What do you see as Israel's most strategic next step? What would you advise Israel to do? Well, thanks for having me on. And I think we have to go back to the first set of strikes earlier in the year where they shot 110 missiles in. And because the U.S. and others help Israel intercept those, the effect was low and the United States implored Israel to not respond in a big way. And Israel led a very, very measured response. So now Iran is back with a much larger strike. And I think what it's going to be hard this time to convince Israel to not have a more forceful reply. There are multiple things they could strike. They could strike that petrochemical infrastructure. They could strike military targets. And of course, they could strike the nuclear program. The U.S. assesses that Israel has destroyed about 50 percent of his ball as arsenal. What's your assessment of Iran's overall military strength, including its proxies, such as his balla, such as Hamas, the Houthis, and the militias in Syria and Iraq? How strong are Israel's immediately surrounding enemies right now? Well, clearly Israel has struck a blow. And the most important blow is they have eliminated essentially the top three echelons of leadership. And so the program is in disarray because the leaders are gone. But if you believe the numbers that people have quoted about, has ballas arsenal and Iran's arsenal, there is quite a few weapons left that could be sent Israel's way. Today we learned that eight IDF soldiers have been killed in Lebanon since the offensive began. Is that what you assess that to be an unusual number for Israel in an offensive like this? Well, it's a tragic number. But remember that urban warfare is the worst. We encountered this in Iraq and other places. When you're doing urban warfare in the modern world, this is the toughest mission you can throw at a land force. So in some places, Israel is going in in very clamped confined spaces and it makes it very tough on their soldiers. So this is not unusual. In fact, frankly, I would have expected the numbers to have been higher. I also want to get your take on Israel's strategy at this stage. IDF forces are making a quick targeted incursions into Lebanon, urban warfare, as you know, then withdrawing. The IDF said today it also clashed with his ballas forces at quote, close range. How do you think Israel is avoiding a full on ground invasion right now doing more of these targeted strikes? Well, I think that we should be happy that that's the attack that they're taking. They're being very surgical. As you said before, they have hit some of the largest caches of weapons and they have hit some of the command and control targets. You were talking at the top of the hour there with folks about the strikes into the heart of Beirut and may I assure you that if they're doing that, they are targeting a very specific target and trying to minimize collateral damage. But remember, just like Hamas, Hezbollah wraps itself in innocence. It intends for an innocence to die. That way the world will control Israel for them. Retired General Philip Bredlov. Thank you so much, General.

text: We begin with breaking news out of the Middle East. This is a significant loss for the Israeli military. Eight, just in the first couple of days of this ground incursion into southern Lebanon, which we should note, it's the first time in 18 years you have to go back to the 2006 war for when Israel last sent significant numbers of ground forces into southern Lebanon and to have this death toll, this early in those operations is a measure of the danger. The danger on the ground there as Israel confronts Hezbollah, not just from the air, as we've seen with a significant number of air strikes, but in ground combat. This comes as Israel is considering retaliation for last night's unprecedented missile attack, some 180 ballistic missiles fired here at Israel, the vast majority of them shot down, but some striking the ground, including around us here in central Tel Aviv last night. Joining me now is Democratic Congressman Jared Mosquist of Florida. He serves on the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Congressman, thanks so much for taking the time. Thanks, Jim. Thanks for having me. First I want to begin with this significant Israeli loss. Our understanding this was in a firefight between an Israeli commando unit and presumably Hezbollah fighters on the other side of the border. This brings back echoes of the 2006 war when Israel suffered significant casualties with an uncertain outcome after the end of that war lasted about a month. I wonder, in your view, does this human cost so early on signal that this operation might be more dangerous than some had imagined? Well, though, I think Israelis know that it's dangerous, but I think they understand that it's more dangerous to allow Iran-Froxies on your border. The appeasement of Iran and its proxies, Hamas and Hezbollah, can no longer stand. We saw this actually just yesterday in Tel Aviv with a terrorist attack that's killing people that were just on the high-speed rail. This mission is going to be dangerous. It is limited in scope. It is trying to push Hezbollah back away from the border so that people in Israel can return to their homes. Remember, Hezbollah has fired 9,000 rockets in the northern Israel. 50,000 plus people have had to flee their homes there. Israel is trying to establish some sort of normalize the situation in the north so that people have been returned to their homes, but also to reestablish deterrence with Iran and its proxies. I understand that I've spent a lot of time in northern Israel and talked to some of those families who have left, but as you know, Israel's track record of attempting exactly the same is spotty at best. It occupied Lebanon for 18 years, from 1982 to 2000. Then again, had the war in 2006, perhaps caused some damage, some losses for Hezbollah lived to survive another day. And I just wonder, given the parallel efforts for some sort of negotiated agreement where perhaps the Lebanese military takes over control for southern Lebanon, might be a more lasting path rather than military action alone. You know, I'm not against that. I think you're right. I think we'll have to get to a negotiated solution at some point. But in the meantime, I think Israel wants to degrade the amount of weapons that are on their border. Tens of thousands of missiles and rockets, pretty advanced stuff like us. And Israel wants to go and degrade some of that capacity before we get to that situation. No one's talking about occupying Lebanon. David, honestly, there's no one I would rather talk to on a morning like this as the world waits for to find out what Israel is going to do here. And I was just reading your piece in the Times. And I actually wanted to ask you, I mean, it seems like the question about how Israel is going to retaliate here does seem to come down to, I mean, there were several Israeli officials that were on with my colleague Wolf Blitzer last night, enough tolly Bennett, former prime minister Michael Orin, the former Israeli ambassador to Washington. Do you think that is on the table here? And what does that mean in terms of escalation? Well, I think it's on the table, Casey. I'm not sure they're going to go that far. And certainly the Biden administration is urging them not to. Well, let's just step back for a moment. The wider war that we were trying to, we spent the past year trying to avoid, it's here. It's upon us, right? I mean, what it meant was don't spread the Gaza war, the war against Hamas elsewhere. And now, of course, we have seen Israel go after Hezbollah, kill its leader. We've seen Israeli attacks and our Houthi attack on Israel and an Israeli counterattack. And now we have seen for the second time in six months Iran sending missiles directly at Israel. They had not really done that since the 1979 Iranian revolution. So on all fronts were there. And then the question is, does Prime Minister Netanyahu choose this moment to escalate further and take out what's the true long term threat to Israel, which of course is the nuclear program? Or does he say, this is going to get us on a cycle we can't stop? And that's the administration to you. And frankly, that's the decision I think we'll know about in the next 24 to 48 hours. Really interesting. And David, you write this. You know, of course, that American officials believe they can persuade Mr. Netanyahu to make his point without setting off a full-blown war. But they can see, you write, that the Israeli Prime Minister may see the next five weeks until the American presidential election as a right moment to try to set that program back by years. After all, former President Donald J. Trump would not complain about a major attack on Iran's military infrastructure and Democrats cannot be afforded to be accused of restraining Israel after Tuesday's missile attack. Can you explain a little bit more about how this interacts with the presidential campaign? Sure. The U.S. has always urged caution that there are diplomatic options here. The cost of striking could include nuclear pollution around Iran. It's a really bad president to set. Let's find some other ways to restrain a program, especially since the Iranians don't seem to be right on top of building a weapon. But now, who's going to go say that? Certainly not Donald Trump, who pulled out of the Iranian nuclear accord and has threatened the Iranians at various moments, and who the Iranians have sent out people to try to assassinate him and broken into his campaign. So no love lost there. And I think for Vice President Harris, it's a really tricky time. If she said after a missile attack like this, really, the Israelis should pair back on this. All right, let's go live to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, where we find former U.S. Defense Secretary Mark Esper, Mr. Secretary, very grateful to have you on this critical morning, as we all wait to see how Israel is going to respond to this. Can you give me a sense of what your view is about the best way for them to move forward?
